I'll second it.

You can unmute. Mindy, could you unmute Mr. Allard?

Did that turn out? Okay. We there? Okay, you're on. Okay, yeah. I just heard of that one amendment that you approved there, box, the size of the box being changed from a four to an eight, eight foot wide in that area?
He was correcting the description of what was approved. It was actually, eight foot wide, four foot high on the plans. It was misdescribed in the in the hearing.

Okay. Oh, so they're talking about opening the area up more so than it was originally planned. Yeah, I I would like to know what changed in that wetlands area from the time that the original builder had it and couldn't build in that area because of it being a wetlands, and then the second owner not building over there because it being a wetlands. And if this was an approved project to put a COVID in back now, why wasn't it approved back when, when the original builder was halted from building there? And the other builder, he didn't build there either. So how did this wetland suddenly not become a wetlands or approve to fill in and put this box in?

I think that that's a misconstrual of the permit application before us. I don't have any direct history of well, first of all, I'm not aware of any prior application to bridge this wetlands. The history of the property, as related by Mr. Person in the hearing, indicates that, of course, it was originally part of a subdivision. And at one point, obviously, there must have been some consideration. There must have been a permit application for an entry or access to the property from was it Old Farms or Times Farm Road? And that was approved, and there was no further action. The present application to bridge the wetlands would allow for development of the property, a subdivision of the property, to construct two residents on that. Now, that is not our concern. Our concern is only that there is an application to bridge a wetlands that involves a watercourse. That's the only thing we're considering in this commission and with this application.

Okay. Okay. The only other thing I was thinking of is, see, that's a clear understanding of what your project is here. In talking to several of the neighbors here, we did notice that when building did start up on that Old Farms Road, a lot of people on this road lost their water and had to come up with new wells. And the water that left over after the project was a lot of rust and some people are finding it very difficult with that. Now that your concern. I know it's just the wetland, but that area is like a big sponge. And if you look at the two brooks that come in or the two water flows that do come into that area, and you look at the amount of water that comes through on a nice rainy day, and look at the amount of water that leaves the property and goes into the other brook on the adjacent side, you'll see it's about a trickle compared to what comes in. So that water is basically sitting there and soaking into the ground. Is that gonna affect my groundwater at some point or anybody around me?

If we can say clearly that it's not going to, I understand that the bigger hole that you're gonna put in there, the eight by four is much better than the four by eight, and it will flow, and it probably won't flood my backyard, or it may, we don't know yet. But there's just a few questions as far as that wetland and that being, that an aquifer, is that filling an aquifer? Where is that water actually going? I know the person that did the survey of it and thought that it was a good idea to put up this this bridge across there, looked at it in the winter and never really gave consideration to it in the summer or in the time that it was raining to really see what the water was doing. At least that's what he said. He said that he was there in the winter. And I don't know if he'd been back there since. And I don't know if anybody on the board has gone over and actually looked at that land to see if it, what, how it how it how you describe it as otherwise, we just say it's wetland. I noticed when I looked up online that there was a lot of descriptions as to Wetland. Let's see. I just can't find my note. How do like that? But yeah, that's all I was really concerned with. I to me, it really don't matter if there's a house up there or not or two houses up there. What would worry me is if he subdivided

after he already had a house up there because we opened up a way to let him up there, and he put a dozen houses up there right behind us. And, and then there was problems because it was blasting involved with making the other houses. So but that's not you're you're just dealing with wetland. I understand that. But those are just my concerns there. And that's my opinion, and that's what I voiced.
I'll just make one point here that we do, in fact, have record from the ecologist who consulted on that, who provided photographs of streamflow conditions after heavy rainfall. And

the commission did a sidewalk on the property. And so we've seen the area of the crossing as well as a little bit upstream and downstream. Of course, we were constrained by the property boundaries. We didn't have permission to look further upstream or downstream without explicit permission of the property owner. So we were restricted, essentially, to looking at the immediate area of the crossing. But we did see where the intermittent water courses flowed, and as they said, the photographs that were submitted on part of the testimony clearly showed the conditions under what I would take to be a flow following a heavy rain event, and including the two water courses that converge and the area below the proposed crossing where the two water courses converge into sort of meander before they again converge to a single watercourse that runs down to the Hawk River. So yeah, we are cognizant of that. Oh, very good, very good. Okay, okay. Very good, sir, thank you. You're welcome.

Okay, so any other public comments? I guess we don't have any other public to comment, so I'll move on to item six, all business, and that is, of course, IWWC application twenty-thirty six. Briefly to summarize the conclusion of the discussion at the last meeting, Commissioner Halsey wanted to get back and review, particularly some of the testimony by Hank Gruner, And we also asked for further engineering analysis with regard to the potential for upstream impact, as well as, again, making sure we understood the downstream impact of this proposed crossing. Today, Agent Wagner distributed a letter or a report. Well, let's see now. Its full title is well, it ends in the Review by bhanfield5321. Pdf. So members of the commission should have received that, and I believe that that has been posted online in the record for this application. And I well, let's see here. I don't see engineer Hanfield on the call.
Yeah. You want to I just wanted to let you know it wasn't posted yet online because Oh, it hasn't been posted yet. Late. It came in late this afternoon.

That's what I figured. Okay. Okay, let's see. I don't see as I said, I don't see any engineer Hanfield on this. I guess let me pull that document up on my other screen here. It's an extensive analysis. There were two points that I noted. One, I see that engineer Bushnell is on the call. Maybe he can explain this to us. A comment sorry, too many files and not enough organization. Okay, there was one comment oh, great, thank you. Thank you, Joe. One comment in item number two of the report, it says that the hydraulic grade line for one hundred year storm well below the 52 hydraulic grade line. Yes, Andrew Bushnell. Thank you. Bushnell Associates. Hydraulic grade line is the level of the water.

Okay. So I guess the question I want to ask here is, let's assume, for the sake of assumption, the improbable event that both culverts get completely blocked and the crossing acts as a dam. My take on that is that water would flow over the dam before it backed up. Correct.

Okay, to the level of the property at 52. Okay. Now, of course, the other comment I have is essentially, Andrew Hanfield would like more information. So the question is then, can that information be provided based on the study so far? Yes, yeah. It can be.

Okay. So we should be able to get a clear answer to the question of whether or not there would be significant upstream effects, with an E, from this project? Correct. Okay. Regrettably, we don't have those answers right now. And so I have to ask members of the commission if they are satisfied with the information provided to date. And if not, what further do they require?

Chairman Elliott, this is Larson. I guess what I would like is the information provided in the letter wasn't provided or wasn't assessed by Mr. Hanfield. He has a bunch of other questions but we asked Mr. Hanfel for his assessment on the upstream. We don't have it yet. I would like to get his buy in. If he were satisfied that everything was good based on the one hundred year storm at 52 Pine Ridge Drive. I think he should have said that in his letter, but he didn't. He asked for more data and he specifically did not answer the question we asked him.
I take your point. Okay, any other comments or information that might be required?

One other comment on that, Chairman Elliott, is do we need to reopen the public hearing so we can have the information once we get it in the public record so that it can be part of the decision process?

Well, it be on the record as part of our deliberations as commission. So no, I don't think and since the information was specifically or requested by the commission, we would not need a further hearing. The hearing did allow for public input and comment. And as an informational process, further information can be gathered without having to go to a hearing, especially when it's information specifically requested by the commission. Commissioner Hallisey. Yes.

You, I think, alluded to a desire to review some of the comments that were made both in the hearing, I think, and during our regular meeting process. Have you been able to do that? And were there questions still pending from your

point of view? I did review the letters from both environmental consultants. And I, I mean, I do have a concern that the town's consultant appears to still be concerned. But there was no definitive direction from Hank that I could see other than a bridge spanning the entire stream crossings. So I'm okay with what I've reviewed. Yes, thank you for the opportunity. Okay. Any other questions or comments from the commission?

Chairman Elliott, I do have two other comments that probably aren't pertinent to the discussion, but make the drawings complete. And on the site plan, I think it's page five of six, it wasn't clear to me that the orientation of the large four by eight foot culvert is properly oriented on the drawing. I think it's consistent with what the minutes originally reflected. And the size in there, well actually it says three inches by eight inches. Sure that was a typo, should have been three by eight. But we've been talking about four by eight. And so I would like to make sure that the drawings reflect what we're all agreeing to as far as proposed mitigation
of the storm water.
So Andrew Bushnell again, it's three foot because we're filling in a foot of it to maintain the natural channel bed for army corps requirements. So it's three foot clear, you know.

Okay, I understand. The other thing that I would ask you to take a look at is it looked like the topography numbers, there's a disconnect when we go from the driveway to the main site. It goes from like 196 to 300 feet. Yeah.

Chairman Elliott, this is Eric Liteska. Was hoping I could speak for a couple of minutes. Sure. Okay. So I was just hoping it would be helpful for a moment to kind of go through a little bit of the history of the design and explain how we've kind of arrived at the design that we have and how it's conformed to the concerns that Mr. Gruner, the herpetologist, as well as the consulting engineer, Hanfield, have gotten, you know, their input. We've really been trying as we've gone along here to respond directly to their concerns. And because this has taken place over the course of several months, I was hoping it would be thought of as kind of helpful to put it all together and explain how we are where we are today. I do appreciate, by the way, the commission's accommodation there to have a special meeting.

But going back a little while here, you know, this is actually almost to the day, a year since the first time we came before the commission. We showed a very early conceptual plan. The commission was nice enough, kind enough to listen to what our thoughts were and give us some, early thoughts. I went back and looked at the, the minutes of that meeting and, Chairman Lally said, well, know, of course we were advised we needed a permit for the crossing and that, you know, decisions were made based on the impact of the wetlands. Chairman Lally said that the design of the crossing would have to ensure that there was no flooding onto adjacent properties. She was thinking ahead obviously since that that came up a while later, and is exactly what we're focused on now. She also said that the Commission would like any plan to be as environmentally conservative as possible. She concluded by saying that, based on what was presented there were certainly solutions. We acquired the land a few months later. We, we immediately started working on delineating the wetlands down in this area a little bit better than they had been and then started designing the crossing with, Mr. Bushnell. And then eventually we ended up, you know, after Mr. Gruner submitted his report, we started working with, George Logan, who started doing direct, very direct assessments of the impact locally

upstream, downstream from an ecological perspective, and then also from a wet stream, from a wetlands perspective. Mr. Hanfield also started looking at our report and then, and, or looking at our, you know, application and then advised, recommended that we start talking to the, Army Corps of Engineers, which of course we did. It was a little bit hard to get in touch with them, but eventually we did get, we did connect with somebody there and indeed they informed us that this crossing was going to be in their jurisdiction. And we are going to, you know, we're in the process of doing, getting a general permit from them. We've also modified the plans. Their requirements for stream crossings, even though this is an intermittent stream, they consider this a stream and they have, standards that we're, you know, that you should meet when you're, when you're crossing something in their jurisdiction. So we modified the, modified the plans to meet their requirements. And then of course, we've also added in the so called icing on the cake. We've added the mitigation

elsewhere on the property. We're going to remove invasive species, plant species and plant, you know, something better to be growing in a wetlands area. Now there's still work that Mr. Bushnell is going to do to work with Mr. Hanfield. So I'm not going to talk about the, you know, the flow dynamics, so the capacity of the system and the potential upstream impact. So I do want Mr. Allard to know that, you know, we've heard him, we take what he's saying very seriously, and we would, you know, we're being very careful about the design, for that reason. Want, like Mr. Gruner, and since Commissioner Hallisey mentioned, his report and his opinion, If you read Mr. Gruner's report, he had two, he obviously, his primary recommendation was a bridge really elevating above the channel totally, to minimize the impact.

But a secondary recommendation that he made was not dissimilar to what we have now. He recommended one open box or, open bottom culvert and he recommended placing it on the Eastern Channel, the Eastern stream bed. And the reason for that most likely was because it's wider and he's concerned, about channelization of the water. What our design is, is one box culvert, which is a little bit different than an open bottom in that, we we've got to restore the stream bed afterwards, but it is part of our design to put, the stream material back into it. It will function like an open bottom culvert. And now it's on the Western Channel, not the Eastern Channel. And the reason for that is our, consulting ecologists and engineer agreed that there's a larger watershed on that side and that if animals were to, you know, small, mid sized wildlife were to approach the crossing, they were more likely to prefer a flatter gradient. And that's where that, it's steeper on the other side, on the Eastern Channel. So for those two reasons, it did make sense to put box on that side. Now it also happens that that's the side right up against the properties on Pine Ridge Drive. So if there is some risk of obstruction or other things that would cause backup,

they've been minimized by us moving it and putting it on that side. Now, just to address that last, the channelization, the thing that Mr. Gruner, you know, has brought up, revisited a few times. I mean, would just ask the commission to go back to, the first report submitted by our, consultant, Mr. Logan. There's photos. If you don't recall them, revisit the report and look at them. Immediately south of the site of the crossing, the water, the water, and the stream beds like converge under, under really wet conditions. The important part of our design, think on the side where there's still a three foot round pipe, which by the way will be embedded, is at the part where the water, the part where the water exits is going to have riprap, right? And it's the, at the, the direct purpose of the riprap is to dissipate the energy of the water flowing out of it, slow the velocity, and spread it back out over the area. If you look, if you look at the plans, you can see that it's wider than, it's far wider than where the water just exits. It's really got the purpose of spreading it back out to an area similar to what, the footprint of the bed was to begin with. And the recurring, you know, the recurring discussion about the bridge, I just want to revisit it one more time and, you know, it was either in the public hearing or in the comments afterward,

that the Army Corps of Engineers best management practices were read from. Now it is an independent jurisdiction from the Andover Commission, right? An independent jurisdiction that we are going through a permit process with separately. And it is true that if you read the publication from the New England District of the Army Corps, that spans are the preferred method for crossings. However, if you read a footnote, the first time the word spans appears, there's a footnote that says three sided and open bottom culverts are included in definition of span. So ours is a box culvert, and that again is a little bit different, right? We will have to

restore the stream bed after we, you know, dig it and drop the box culvert in. However, I think it's really important for the commission to understand that it's not the army corps position. They are not saying that bridges are preferred, spans are preferred, not bridges. And we really, we, you know, it's confirmation of that. We've, we've talked to the, to the army corps. They're familiar with what we're doing. Nobody has even suggested at all that a bridge spanning the whole channel is, you know, is what we should be doing here instead of the crossing. They've informed us that the culvert is what we to do to comply with the practices. And finally, you know, I apologize for talking for a while here, you know, having a little bit of time to think about some of the things that were said in the public hearing and then afterwards, you know, we are not aware of, and in the last year, no one in the commission, no one consulting on the application, has brought to our attention any applicable

statutes or regulations that prohibit the construction of a crossing like the one that we're proposing based on the amount of square footage of the impacted area or the volume of fill that has to come into construct it. These are of course important considerations, or, criteria for determining, you know, regulatory jurisdiction methods, and maybe most importantly, the amount of scrutiny that should be applied to an application. And indeed, just as you would expect, you know, the moment that our application was submitted, this commission, a motion was made and was carried to consider this a significant activity. And since then we have complied, you know, we have cooperated, we have acted in good faith, substantial changes have been made to the design after careful analysis and consideration from our professionals

and, in direct response to the concerns made by, you know, the folks who are consulting on behalf of the commission. Our construction budget for the crossing has nearly tripled from where it started, and we believe the pro-, we believe the process the commission has taken us through has been thorough and professional, and we believe it, we just believe that the design as it is exceeds the town's, regulations, and strikes an appropriate balance between the cost of constructing a driveway for a, to serve one household with, the appropriate measures to mitigate the risks, and minimize the impact. So I mean, I'm sorry for taking a few minutes here, but I really, this having taken place over a long time, I thought it would be helpful to summarize the back and forth that's been going on, for even for the commission, it's, you know, it's probably difficult to always remember everything that's going on with every application, but we hope that you'll just bear in mind that we've been working diligently to try and address the concerns
of the commission and then of course the members of the public here who's attended the public hearing. So thank you. Thank

you, Eric. Yeah, you're right. It has been an iterative process. There has been a lot of back and forth. And you're quite right. This is a permittable type of activity. I, in fact, had a little back and forth with, Agent Wagner, and I think that perhaps by the next hearing we might have some comparison. Unfortunately, my personal records don't go back that far, and my institutional memory is only a couple of years here, but certainly we have permitted wetland crossings for driveways, including one of the early ones that I worked on, a permit for a driveway on Townsend Road that also involved crossing an intermittent water course. Now, a smaller one, a lot less engineering involved in the crossing, but still comparable on the order of magnitude area. And so from that point of view, yes, you're quite right. This is an activity that is permittable under our regulations. And I guess the questions are all really related to both the environmental impact and the how shall I say the environmental sensitivity of this particular crossing as it happens to be pretty closely adjacent to the Hop River. So, you know, with that in mind, obviously, I think more questions have been raised than you might see for a less impacting

application. And again, I think it seems to be coming down to just this one last piece of information where we would like to have a direct answer from our consulting engineer regarding the upstream impacts. And I sincerely hope that at the special meeting, will be able to resolve this issue and make an informed decision on your application. Again, while we're at it, will ask Agent Wagner see if he can delve into the town hall files and look for reasonably comparable crossings in terms of the number, at least the square footage impacted and the kinds of engineering solutions that have gone into it. Again, as I say, my institutional memory is too short to serve for that purpose.
Mr. Chairman, Elliot, would I be able to ask a couple of follow-up questions since we did have the opportunity to listen? Sure. Ahead. The

first question, and you maybe covered it, is I was interested in why you went with the box culvert instead of the three sided thing. And I forget the name of it, but you made that distinction and I didn't know why.

George, feel free to. Yeah, I can answer that. The four sided box culvert is a it's more available than the three sided there's only one or two manufacturers in this area that do that and. To be honest, the four sided. Doctor. Box culvert is structurally stronger.

Okay. And my second question is, we've continued this dialogue in refining how we're going. I'll just do the half interval search one more time. I agree that probably the bridge is not cost effective for one house. But I am wrestling with Mr. Bruner's comments concerning the flow and the siltation and the erosion in that. And so one of the alternatives that we alluded to during the public hearing but we didn't really discuss would have been to have two box culverts. And that way we can put one where Mr. Bruner thought it should be and one where you thought it should be. And that would really you know, maximize the span without going to the cost of the bridge. And you don't need to have an answer to that tonight. But that's one of the things that I'm wrestling with is we're trying to come up with what the best proposal is here to do all of those things.

I believe that was addressed. I won't trust my own recollection, but I think Zener that Bushnell commented on that proposal. Do you recall that comment about why not two blocks over it instead of one in terms of the impact on stream flow and so forth?
I'm trying to remember. I don't remember right off the top of my head. No, sorry.

I think, I mean, part of this of course is cost. These culverts are very expensive but I don't think that there is, much gained in terms of, capacity and performance of the system to sort of maintain the integrity of the stream channel other than just having a wider spot in one place where we're, you know, where we're gonna allow the water to flow through. I mean, we are like well beyond the hundred year in terms of flow, right? So the only benefit is of going to the larger culvert on the second side is really just preserving stream bed even though,
right? I mean, that what it boils down to? Mean Just preserving some more stream bed width, right, compared to the three foot culvert, sure.

I understand. So I still do have concerns, haven't certainly made up my mind one way or the other yet. But I did go back and review the photos that were submitted on that.
